evals.prompt: I run growth at Hoverlane, a hosted log-pipeline product. Since we launched 19 months ago we've had 8,412 signups and 19 of those people pay us. That's 0.23%, and every SaaS benchmark post I read says 3-5% is normal, so we're roughly 20x off. Our VP of Engineering wants to spend the whole quarter rebuilding onboarding. Before I greenlight that, is conversion actually our problem? Two extra details that may or may not matter: 74% of our accounts still have exactly one developer in them sixty days after signup, and the 0.23% is computed by dividing everyone who has ever paid us by everyone who has ever signed up.
evals.expected_output: A reframing that rejects the blended benchmark row and the lifetime user-level ratio, re-specifies the measurement, runs the friction gates, and locates the problem as spread rather than conversion.
expectations: States that developer-focused companies show a median free-to-paid conversion of roughly 5%, about half the median of non-developer-focused companies, and attributes it to the Lenny's Newsletter free-to-paid conversion survey.
Identifies the 3-5% figure as the freemium pure-self-serve band and notes it assumes a different measurement from the one the user ran.
Rejects the user's lifetime all-signups-ever ratio as the wrong measurement, and states that a lifetime ratio flatters or distorts any product whose signups grew.
Gives the measurement definition the published bands assume: accounts that begin paying within their first six months divided by accounts created in the measurement window.
Requires the recomputation to be done by cohort.
Requires the recomputation to be done at account level rather than per individual user.
Names the 74% single-developer figure as a spread problem rather than a conversion problem.
Runs or asks for the three friction gates by name - entry, value and spread - instead of moving straight to onboarding work.
Requires each gate to be answered with evidence such as a cold run of the company's own onboarding, not with an opinion or belief.
Declines to endorse the onboarding rebuild as the first action on the evidence given.
Labels each number it uses as either sourced, with its source and measurement definition, or self-set.
Does not assert that a 0.23% conversion rate proves the funnel is broken.

evals.prompt: Turnstile Metrics here, we sell a hosted metrics backend. 4,100 active accounts, average revenue per account is $31 a month, and 96% of accounts have exactly one developer in them. Our board just approved headcount for two account executives starting in Q1; fully loaded, each one costs us about $210,000 a year. My co-founder's argument is 'the enterprise demand is obviously there, we just never asked for it.' I'm not sure. What should I tell the board next week?
evals.expected_output: An arithmetic answer using the 4x fully-loaded-cost test, with the opposite risk held in view, concluding against the hire as specified or naming what would change it.
expectations: Applies an explicit sales-economics test requiring a salesperson added to a self-serve motion to return roughly 4x their fully loaded cost in incremental revenue, and attributes it to The Transition (Lenny's Newsletter).
States the resulting bar as roughly $840,000 of incremental revenue per rep per year against the $210,000 fully loaded cost given.
Tests the bar by multiplying a qualified-account volume by a realistic deal size, rather than arguing the motion philosophically.
Concludes on the evidence given that the two-AE hire is not yet supported, or names the specific conditions that would make it supported.
States that account rollup must exist before any motion with a human in the loop is available.
Holds the opposite risk in view rather than only arguing against sales: names that waiting too long lets sales-assisted competitors firewall a self-serve-only product out of enterprise segments.
Cites Dropbox as the named casualty of adding sales too late.
Quotes or paraphrases Pete Kazanjy's warning never to mistake lead generation for the business, and attributes it to him.
Notes that self-serve at roughly $19-29 a month is lead generation while the business is the far larger contract.
Names Datadog and New Relic as developer companies that nonetheless run sales organizations.
Frames the decision as when a human enters the loop, not whether one ever does.
Warns that reps hired against a majority single-developer account base will find nothing to work and start contacting signups, damaging the free surface.
Does not recommend hiring both account executives in Q1 on the numbers given.

evals.prompt: Quick one. We're a dev tool, a CI caching service, around 2,300 free accounts. I read that if you contact a lead within 5 minutes you're 21x more likely to qualify them. I want to wire a Slack alert on every signup so someone emails them within the same minute. Our head of sales is already building the automation and wants copy from me by Thursday. What should the email say, and should we just call them instead?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build signup-triggered outreach, with the statistic's provenance named, replaced by an account-level threshold rule with an hours-scale window and a written do-not-contact line.
expectations: Refuses to build same-minute or signup-triggered human outreach.
Identifies the 5-minute / 21x statistic as coming from inbound form-fill research in sales-led funnels rather than from developer product usage.
Notes the statistic is usually cited to a vendor blog rather than to the underlying study.
States that importing that statistic into a developer motion amounts to contacting on signup.
Names contacting on signup as the behaviour this audience punishes hardest, or as teaching developers that the free tier is bait.
Moves qualification to account level rather than per individual signup.
Proposes a written qualification threshold expressed as a single sentence the team can apply without interpretation.
Sets the response window for qualified accounts in hours rather than in days or in minutes.
Labels the hours-not-days window as this skill's own baseline with no study behind it, not as an industry standard.
Requires an explicit written do-not-contact line covering accounts below the threshold.
Replaces the generic sales email with a technical offer such as a limits, quota, architecture or migration conversation, and rejects openers of the '15 minutes to learn about your needs' shape.

evals.prompt: At Clearmast, developer feature-flagging, we built a lead score last quarter: pricing page visit = 10 points, marketing email open = 5, docs visit = 8, signed up in the last 7 days = 15. Anything over 60 points goes to our SDR queue. It is not working. Reply rates are around 2% and people are visibly annoyed on Twitter. Last month one regional bank produced 40 separate signups and our SDR sent 40 separate emails to them. Help me re-tune the weights so we route better.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the scoring model itself, replaced by account rollup plus the three signal families ordered by intent, with boundary contact strongest.
expectations: Rejects re-tuning the point weights as the wrong project.
Names the scoring model as the MQL construction rather than a genuine product-qualified-lead model.
States that email opens and pricing-page visits measure marketing exposure, not a developer's product usage.
Treats the bank's 40 signups as one account rather than forty leads.
Requires usage to be rolled up to an account before any qualification rule is applied.

Names at least two account rollup sources from the set: organization or workspace object, license or API key or install ID, email domain, self-reported company at signup, enrichment from IP or company data.
Advises combining at least two rollup sources rather than relying on a single one.
Introduces the three signal families by name: depth, spread and boundary contact.
Orders the three families by increasing intent, with boundary contact the strongest.
Justifies boundary contact as strongest because it maps directly onto the paid boundary the business model defined.
Gives concrete boundary-contact examples such as SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit log, repeated rate or seat limit hits, a security questionnaire, SOC 2 report, DPA, or billing and procurement pages.
Distinguishes depth without spread, which usually means a solo power user, from spread without depth, which usually means an evaluation that has not committed.

Recommends having a human read raw new signups in an internal channel for a few weeks before building any scoring system, or cites Zapier's four sales-assist qualification signals as a published cross-check.

evals.prompt: Parapet is a self-hosted policy engine for Kubernetes. To get any value at all you deploy our admission controller into a cluster, which means a platform engineer has to approve it and apply it, and the product does nothing useful until three or more services are onboarded to it. Constraints from my CTO, stated as non-negotiable: no new headcount this calendar year, our board meets in 10 weeks and needs to see revenue movement by then, and we will not hand a reseller or a marketplace any margin. We have no free tier today. Everyone on the team keeps saying 'we should do PLG.' Design our go-to-market.
evals.expected_output: A gate-by-gate analysis that rules out bottom-up, deletes two motions on the stated constraints, notes motion 2 has nothing to convert, and surfaces the resulting contradiction instead of picking silently.
expectations: Fails the entry gate explicitly, naming the cluster deployment and the platform engineer's approval as mandatory steps between arrival and first value.
States that a failing entry gate rules out bottom-up self-serve outright.
Fails or partially fails the value gate, naming that value only appears once three or more services are onboarded, which is team-scale rather than single-developer.
States that a failing value or spread gate means a hybrid motion - developer entry with a human-assisted or platform-level conversion - not a pure bottom-up one.
Deletes top-down with developer proof on the no-new-headcount constraint.
Deletes ecosystem-mediated on the refusal to give up margin.
Records each deleted motion together with the specific constraint that ruled it out.
Refuses to leave a ruled-out motion parked at the bottom of the menu as a lesser option.
States that developer-influenced sales has nothing to convert here because no base of free accounts exists yet.
Surfaces that the stated constraints eliminate every available motion, and names which constraint must be relaxed rather than silently picking one anyway.
Presents two or three candidate motions rather than a single recommendation.
Commits to at most one primary motion and at most one secondary motion.
Does not recommend 'PLG' or a free tier without first addressing the failed entry gate.

evals.prompt: Reviewing our GTM memo before it goes to the board on Friday. The motion section reads, in full: 'Fernwake runs a PLG motion with an enterprise sales layer for larger accounts. We will also pursue cloud marketplace and partner channels opportunistically.' Our head of revenue thinks it's crisp and wants to ship it. I think something is off but I can't articulate what. Can you tighten the wording?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that three motions are declared as one, with the one-primary rule enforced, a rejected-motions section demanded, and the taxonomy's published-versus-synthesized status stated.
expectations: Identifies that three motions are declared as one and that no decision has actually been made.
States the rule of exactly one primary motion and at most one secondary motion that stacks on it.
Explains that two primaries mean the team will argue about which funnel every account belongs to.
Flags 'opportunistically' as how a motion with no owner gets written down.
Requires a 'Rejected motions' section naming each rejected motion and the constraint that ruled it out.
Distinguishes a motion blocked only for now, which belongs in the memo's revisit triggers, from one rejected outright.
Names the four motions it works from: bottom-up self-serve, developer-influenced sales, top-down with developer proof, and ecosystem-mediated.
States that this four-motion taxonomy is the skill's own synthesis and not a published framework.

Gives the published vocabulary underneath as two independent axes - product-led versus sales-led, and top-down versus bottom-up - plus sales assist, attributed to the Lenny's Newsletter study of GTM motions across 30 B2B SaaS companies.
Declines to fix the section by rewording alone.
Requires the memo section to name the money path and the prerequisite that must be true for the chosen motion.

evals.prompt: Ridgepin sells an API gateway. We have a free tier with about 12,000 accounts on it. Here's the thing: 100% of our revenue has come from our two SDRs cold-emailing people who signed up for that free tier. Nobody has ever upgraded on their own. The upgrade button works, people just don't press it. Every quarter our growth lead and our sales lead have the exact same fight about 'fixing the PLG funnel', and we're going into planning again next week. What should I do differently this time?
evals.expected_output: The motion named as bottom-up lead gen with its source, the PLG label rejected, and an explicit keep-or-convert decision required instead of more funnel work.
expectations: Names the motion as bottom-up lead generation: a sales-led company whose free product exists to feed leads rather than revenue.
Attributes the term to the Lenny's Newsletter study of GTM motions across 30 B2B SaaS companies.
States that the team is not running product-led growth despite calling it that.
States that naming the motion correctly is what ends the recurring argument, rather than more funnel work.
Notes that a team can run bottom-up lead gen for years while believing it runs product-led growth.
Requires an explicit decision to either keep the motion and staff it honestly, or convert it, rather than continuing to optimize an unnamed one.
Flags contacting the whole free base as burning the free surface's reputation with a developer audience.
Requires a written do-not-contact line for accounts below a threshold.
Requires the qualification threshold to be written as one sentence naming an owner and a response window.
Requires account-level rollup rather than treating each free signup as an individual lead.
Labels every number it introduces as either sourced with its source, or self-set.

evals.prompt: Auventa, we do distributed tracing. Our biggest customer is a regional bank: three engineering teams, about $48,000 a year, signed 14 months ago on a company credit card and later moved to an invoice. The staff engineer who brought us in left the company five weeks ago and the account has gone completely silent since. Renewal is in four months. Our head of sales wants to offer them 25% off for a two-year commitment to 're-engage and lock them in', and then pitch that same discount to other departments to expand. Sound plan?
evals.expected_output: Discount rejected as an expansion lever, the vector named with a trigger and owner, multi-threading and standardization applied, and procurement re-entry anticipated.
expectations: Rejects the 25% discount as an expansion lever.
States that expansion produced by price changes or by usage the customer did not choose is deferred churn, not expansion.
Names the expansion vector in play - more teams in the same company - rather than treating expansion generically.
Assigns that vector both a firing trigger and a named owner.
Names at least one further expansion vector from the set: more developers on the same team, more workload per user, more product surface.
Names the standardization decision by a platform or architecture group as the gate on continued growth in a large account.
States that the champion enablement pack has to survive an architecture review rather than a hallway conversation.
Applies the multi-threading rule of a second technical advocate plus one manager-level contact.
States that both multi-threaded contacts must have seen value with their own eyes.
Treats the departed champion as simultaneously a risk in this account and a warm entry at their new employer.
Warns about procurement re-entry: the second, larger purchase can trigger the security review, legal pass and vendor onboarding that the original credit-card purchase skipped.
Requires that paperwork be prepared before the expansion conversation rather than during it.
Does not present quarterly business reviews or renewal-timed upsell calls as the expansion mechanism.

evals.prompt: Stavemill, bottom-up developer tool, mostly small teams paying by card. Our net revenue retention came in at 103% for the trailing twelve months. One of our investors said flatly that 'good SaaS is 120% plus' and now our CEO wants to build an upsell motion this quarter. Separately: we report 1,900 seats to the board, which is every seat ever provisioned across our paying accounts. Our standing board metrics are signups, MAU, ARR and NPS. Is 103% actually bad?
evals.expected_output: The bottom-up retention row applied instead of the enterprise one, provisioned seats rejected for active seats, and the four lagging board metrics replaced with a small leading-indicator set.
expectations: States that the published 12-month band for a bottom-up product puts 'good' near 100% and 'great' near 120%.
Contrasts that with the enterprise SaaS band of roughly 110% good and 130% great.
Concludes that 103% is normal or good for the motion the company actually runs, not a failure.
Attributes the retention bands to the Lenny's Newsletter retention benchmark post.
Gives the definition of net revenue retention as a cohort's MRR today divided by that same cohort's MRR twelve months ago.
Rejects reporting provisioned seats and requires active seats to be counted instead.
States that dormant seats predict contraction at renewal.
Identifies signups, MAU, ARR and NPS as lagging or unactionable indicators for this purpose.
Replaces them with a leading-indicator set of five or fewer numbers, all of which move before revenue.
Labels the five-or-fewer cap as this skill's own self-set baseline rather than a published rule.
Gives each proposed indicator a target and a date.
Does not endorse launching an upsell motion purely because 103% sits below 120%.

evals.prompt: Kelbrook sells a secrets-management platform. We only sell top-down: our AE team works CISOs and platform directors, contracts run $180K to $400K, and everything - docs, the API reference, pricing, rate limits, even the error-code pages - sits behind a 'Book a demo' form because our CRO wants every visitor captured as a lead. Two of our last four renewals came in flat or down, and in both cases the customer said some version of 'our engineers never really used it.' I'm the new VP of Product and I start Monday. Where do I begin?
evals.expected_output: Shelfware named as the motion's failure mode, entry design asserted as load-bearing even top-down, the gated surfaces reopened, and post-purchase developer activation set as the leading indicator.
expectations: Names shelfware as the failure mode of a top-down motion: the contract is signed, adoption never happens, and the renewal conversation has no usage to point at.
States that entry design still matters in a top-down motion because developers handed a tool evaluate it the same way as developers who chose it.
States that a bad entry turns handed-a-tool developers into internal opponents.
Requires documentation to be permanently ungated.
Requires pricing detail and limits to be permanently ungated.
Requires error and troubleshooting content to be permanently ungated.
States that gating those surfaces loses technical evaluations silently, because developers evaluate before they will talk to anyone.
Names post-purchase developer activation as this motion's leading indicator - the share of licensed developers actually using the product within a defined window such as 90 days.
Rejects a demo-only enterprise path with no self-serve floor, naming that it leaves the long tail unservable.
Names a concrete first-value moment as an observable event rather than calling it 'activation'.
Counts the mandatory steps a developer must pass before reaching that first-value moment.
Does not accept the lead-capture rationale as a reason to keep documentation gated.

evals.prompt: Need to write our PQL rule today. We're Ostrich Labs, a hosted vector database, roughly 5,600 free accounts. I found a blog post from a much bigger infrastructure company saying their rule is '5 or more seats and 30 days of usage' and I want to just adopt that, since it's battle-tested at their scale. One complication: we have no workspace or organization object in the product, so all we have is the signup email address, and maybe a third of those are gmail.com or similar. Write me the rule.
evals.expected_output: The copied threshold refused, rollup made a build line item with named sources and weaknesses, and a one-sentence rule produced with owner, hours-scale window and do-not-contact line.
expectations: Refuses to copy the other company's threshold, on the grounds that cohort shapes differ too much for the number to transfer.
Requires the threshold numbers to be derived from the accounts that have already converted at this company.
Requires the chosen value to produce a queue the responder can actually clear.
States that account rollup does not exist here, and makes building it a line item of the plan rather than a footnote.
Names email domain as an available but weak rollup source.
Names the specific weaknesses of email domain: free-mail addresses and contractors leak, and subsidiaries fragment.
Names at least two further rollup sources - organization or workspace object, license or API key, self-reported company at signup, or enrichment - and advises combining at least two.
Writes the qualification threshold as a single sentence.
Includes an active-developer count condition in that sentence.
Includes a duration-of-production-usage condition in that sentence.
Includes boundary contact as an alternative qualifying trigger in that sentence.
Names the role who acts on a qualified account and a response window measured in hours.
States explicitly that accounts below the threshold are not contacted by a human.
Labels the numbers in the rule as self-set or derived from the company's own data, and notes that how many active developers an account needs before it converts is not published anywhere.

evals.prompt: Tilcrest makes a CLI for database schema migrations. Our usage splits almost evenly: indie developers and two-person consultancies on our $9/month plan, and platform teams inside insurance companies and banks who want SSO, audit logs and an MSA before they'll touch us. We're about to rebuild onboarding as one flow for everybody, and our board deck reports a single blended free-to-paid conversion number. Our head of growth's position is 'a developer is a developer.' Design the onboarding and tell me what to report.
evals.expected_output: The two audiences ranked rather than averaged, with what is shared and what diverges named, and conversion reported per audience at account level by cohort.
expectations: Refuses to design one entry serving both audiences, stating that an entry built for a hobbyist and an enterprise platform team at once serves neither.
Requires the two paths to be ranked explicitly, with one named primary.
Names what is identical for both: first value must be reachable by one developer working alone.
Names that documentation, limits and pricing detail stay open for both audiences.
Names what differs after the first paid moment: who is contacted, what is offered, and what expansion even means.
States that in individual adoption the user and the payer are the same person, or no purchase exists at all.
States that for the individual-adoption path a human in the loop costs more than the contract.
States that company adoption requires account rollup, a champion enablement pack and procurement paperwork.
Rejects the single blended conversion number and requires conversion to be reported per audience as well as blended.
Notes that larger target customers correlate with lower conversion, so blending the two hides both.
Requires conversion to be measured at account level and by cohort.
Does not conclude that one onboarding flow can be optimized for both segments at once.
